catalog_quote: Petsuk (1978ː26) posits the typical phonological syllable in Khuen monosyllabic morphemes or stressed syllables in polysyllabic morphemes as C(C)V(C)T, that is, a compulsory initial consonant followed by a highly restricted optional second consonant, an obligatory vowel nucleus carrying an obligatory tone followed by an optional consonant final. Note also that the vowel can be the syllabic nasal [m̩]. This structure provides a framework for interpretation of individual segments as described below. Unstressed syllables in polysyllabic morphemes conform to a CVT template where the vowel is normally, but not always, [a] and the tone is also highly restricted but not enough to be considered toneless (Petsuk 1978:28-29).

new_statements.rule_in_words: The source (second-hand from Petsuk 1978) says Khuen polysyllabic morphemes contain stressed syllables with the full C(C)V(C)T template and unstressed, reduced CVT syllables whose vowel is normally [a] with a restricted tone; it does NOT say which position in the word is stressed. (The reduced-[a] syllable pattern is the familiar Southwestern-Tai non-final minor syllable, which would imply final stress, but that placement is an inference, not stated in any page opened.)
new_statements.exceptions: Unstressed-syllable vowel is 'normally, but not always, [a]'; its tone is 'highly restricted but not enough to be considered toneless'. Most polysyllables are loans (Burmese, Pali, Sanskrit, English) per Petsuk 1978:26, though native compounds/reduplications exist.
new_statements.domain_note: Polysyllabic morphemes (word-internal); lexical tone on every full syllable. No phrase-level or citation-form remarks.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources concern Tai Khün/Khuen of Kengtung (Chiang Tung), Shan State, Myanmar = khun1259 [kkh]; Owen's data are from villages around Kengtung (Klang Muong, Baan Veng etc.), the Thai articles add transplanted Khün communities in Chiang Mai (San Pa Tong, San Kamphaeng) and Nan, Thailand -- same language, no separate glottocodes.
